title: Epoxy coating in Rioz: wheels and older parts treated by SAVA
author: Les Caramagnols
excerpt: At SAVA, epoxy coating is not just one more decorative finish. It is used to bring wheels and parts back into service so they can last in real conditions.
content:
In the presentation of its classic-car work, SAVA lists epoxy coating as a restoration step in its own right. That deserves attention because epoxy is often misunderstood. It is sometimes reduced to a prettier finish or a surface effect. Yet on wheels and parts exposed to impacts, rubbing, moisture and road grime, the real value lies first in how well the treatment holds after serious preparation.

The workshop page is clear on that point: blasting, treatment and then epoxy coating on steel or aluminium parts able to withstand curing around 180°C. That technical reminder is enough to place the process properly. This is not a quick disguise, but a restoration chain in which the surface has to be made sound before the final protection is applied.

Why wheels are such good candidates

Wheels concentrate a large share of the visible stress carried by an older car. They take impacts, brake dust, water, periods of storage and sometimes the marks of previous repairs of mixed quality. When the base can still be recovered, a refurbishment followed by epoxy coating makes sense because it brings both a cleaner finish and better resistance in real use.

The examples shown by SAVA on Golf and 4L wheels speak for themselves. What becomes visible is not only an even colour brought back to life. More importantly, the part becomes clean, readable and protected again, ready to return to a restored vehicle without remaining an obvious weak point.

Preparation matters as much as the final layer

In this kind of work, the finish coat does not do everything. If the part remains dirty, contaminated or irregular, no paint will correct the base for long. Blasting, preliminary treatment and defect control are therefore as important as the epoxy itself. That is often where the difference lies between a part that has merely been “redone” and one that has genuinely been brought back into condition.

This logic applies to wheels, but also to other metal components that can take heat and mechanical use. On an older car, it helps move toward a cleaner reassembly with parts that do not clash with the rest of the project.

A finishing process that stays in service of the whole project

At SAVA, epoxy coating seems to keep that proper measure. It appears as a useful step inside a restoration, not as an isolated selling point. That is exactly what one expects from a workshop that also handles mechanics, upholstery and the treatment of smaller parts: the finish should never detach itself from the whole job.

For the broader frame of the workshop, the page SAVA in Rioz gathers the main points. And to understand how this type of finish fits into a larger job, the article on classic car restoration at SAVA is the natural continuation.
